title: Nocturnal animals
titleCn: 夜行动物的生存适应：洞穴蟹与二趾树懒

paragraphs.text: Part four. You will hear a lecture about nocturnal animals. First, you have some times to look at questions thirty-one to forty. Listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
Good morning, everyone.
Today, I will discuss the fascinating world of nocturnal animals, focusing on the adaptations that enable them to thrive in darkness.
Many species have evolved unique features to help them survive and avoid competition or predation at night.
To begin, one of the most notable evolutionary trends among nocturnal species is the loss of certain organs that are no longer needed.
Over time, some animals have developed alternative ways to navigate and interact with their surroundings, making specific body parts redundant.
A great example is the cave crab, which has completely lost its eyes.
Since it resides in deep, dark environments where light is scarce, vision is unnecessary, and instead, these crabs rely on other senses to detect movement and find food.
This is just one example of how nature optimizes an animal's physiology according to its environment.
Now, let's turn our attention to a nocturnal mammal that exhibits several remarkable adaptations, the two-toed sloth.

Unlike its three-toed counterpart, this species has a far more varied diet. The key reason for this is that it forages primarily at night, which allows it to avoid competing with other animals for food resources.
As a result, two-toed sloths have access to a wider range of plant species and even some small animals, unlike their more restricted relatives.
Another crucial adaptation in two-toed sloths is their highly flexible head, which allows them to observe their environment more effectively.
Unlike many other mammals, these sloths can rotate their heads at a much greater angle, providing them with a broader field of vision.
This increased mobility is advantageous in detecting predators and potential threats, even in dense forest environments.
Additionally, these animals possess the ability to regulate their body temperature based on surrounding conditions.

Unlike many mammals that maintain a constant internal temperature, two-toed sloths can adjust theirs depending on factors such as humidity and ambient temperature. This helps them conserve energy, which is essential to survival given their slow metabolic rate.

Furthermore, a rather unusual but effective form of camouflage assists them in blending into their habitat. Their fur hosts algae, which give it a greenish tint, allowing them to merge seamlessly with tree foliage. This mutualistic relationship benefits both organisms. The sloth gains improved concealment from predators, while the algae receive shelter and nutrients from the sloth's fur.
Moving on, let's discuss another nocturnal species, the North Island brown kiwi, which has developed distinct adaptations to survive in its habitat.
This bird has evolved to be active at night primarily to evade predators, particularly a species of eagle that once posed a significant threat to it.
By becoming nocturnal, kiwis minimize encounters with these formidable hunters and improve their chances of survival.
Interestingly, kiwis do not rely much on vision as their eyes are poorly adapted for detailed sight, especially when it comes to perceiving colors.
Unlike many birds that use their eyesight to locate food, kiwis compensate with an exceptional sense of smell.
Their nostrils are located at the tip of their long beaks, a rare feature among birds, allowing them to detect insects and worms hidden beneath the soil.
This heightened olfactory ability is a crucial survival tool in the darkness.
Another surprising trait of kiwis is the size of their eggs.

When compared to their body proportions, kiwi eggs are exceptionally large. In fact, a single egg can take up about twenty percent of the mother's body, making it one of the most disproportionate egg sizes in the animal kingdom.
This unusual adaptation ensures that kiwi chicks hatch in a well-developed state, giving them a better chance of surviving in the wild.

Finally, let's turn our attention to bats, the only mammals capable of sustained flight. One of their most remarkable adaptations is the presence of specialized skin on their ears, which enhances their ability to use echolocation.
Bats emit high-frequency sounds that bounce off objects, allowing them to interpret the returning echoes and navigate through complete darkness.
This skill is especially crucial for hunting flying insects, which they track with astonishing precision.
An additional fascinating feature of bats relates to their sleeping posture.
Unlike most animals that rest on solid ground, bats sleep while hanging upside down.
This is made possible because their claws remain securely hooked onto surfaces due to gravity.

Unlike human hands, which require muscle effort to grip objects, bats' tendons naturally lock in place, ensuring that they do not fall while resting. This efficient mechanism enables them to conserve energy and remain safely out of reach of predators.

In conclusion, nocturnal animals have developed an array of specialized traits that allow them to thrive in environments where others struggle. Whether it's losing unnecessary organs, adjusting metabolism, or relying on echolocation, these adaptations highlight the incredible diversity and resilience of life in the natural world.
